title: Matter cycling in ecosystems
keyIdea: Matter moves round an ecosystem in a cycle and is used again and again. Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air and water and minerals from the soil, and build them into their bodies. Animals eat plants (or other animals), so the matter moves into them. Animal droppings, dead animals and dead plants are food for decomposers such as fungi and bacteria, helped by worms. Decomposers break them down and give carbon dioxide and water back to the air and nutrients back to the soil, where plants take them in again. Rotting does not destroy matter; it only moves it. Without decomposers, dead matter would pile up and plants would run out of nutrients.
familyTip: Look under a pile of old leaves or a rotting log together. Find the fungi, woodlice and worms, and the dark crumbly soil underneath. Ask: where did last year's leaves go?

visual.caption: What job does each living thing do in the cycle? Drag each one to a box, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: carry matter round a cycle, rot 100 g of leaves, run sealed gardens with and without decomposers, fill a compost bin, follow one atom.

kid: Everything is made of matter. Grass takes in a gas called carbon dioxide from the air. It also takes water and minerals from the soil. It uses them to build its leaves and roots.
A rabbit eats the grass, so the matter is now in the rabbit. The rabbit leaves droppings. One day it dies. Fungi, bacteria and worms feed on the droppings and the body. They are called decomposers.
Decomposers break dead things down. They give carbon dioxide and water back to the air. They leave nutrients in the soil. Then new grass takes them in. The same matter goes round and round.

Rotting does not make matter vanish. When 100 g of leaves rot, the 100 g goes into the soil and the air. If there were no decomposers, dead leaves would pile up. The soil would run out of nutrients, and plants would stop growing.
adult: Ages 10 to 11. NGSS 5-LS2-1 asks pupils to develop a model to describe the movement of matter among plants, animals, decomposers and the environment. It pairs with 5-LS1-1 (plants get the materials they need for growth chiefly from air and water) and with the Grade 5 idea that matter is conserved. In the National Curriculum in England the same ideas run through Year 6 living things and the Key Stage 3 nutrient and carbon cycles.

The lab keeps one rule in view: matter moves but is not used up. Pupils carry a matter marker round air and soil, grass, a rabbit and decomposers; rot a 100 g leaf pile and watch the leaves, soil and air bars always add to 100 g (a simple model, not measured data); run two sealed gardens with and without decomposers; sort a compost bin; and name the process at each move of one carbon atom.

Common mistakes. Many children think rotting destroys matter or turns it into energy, that decomposers are only harmful 'germs', that plants get their mass from the soil, and that soft things like plastic bags will rot. Some think matter flows only one way, as in a food chain, and stops at the top predator. Ask 'where do the atoms go next?' at each step to catch these.

practice.prompt: A leaf falls and rots on the ground. Where does its matter go?
choices: Into the soil and the air
practice.hint: Decomposers feed on the leaf. What do they give back?
practice.explain: Decomposers break the leaf down. They give carbon dioxide and water to the air and leave nutrients in the soil. Nothing vanishes.

practice.prompt: {a} g of dead leaves rot completely. In a simple model, {b} g goes into the air. How many grams go into the soil?
practice.hint: Matter is not lost. The air part and the soil part add up to the whole.
practice.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} g goes into the soil, so {b} + {=a-b} = {a} g. The total stays the same.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a decomposer?
practice.hint: Decomposers feed on dead things and waste.
practice.explain: Mushrooms are fungi, and fungi feed on dead wood and leaves. Rabbits are consumers and grass is a producer.

practice.prompt: A sealed jar garden has {a} nutrient units in its soil and no decomposers. The plant uses 3 units each season. How many units are left after 2 seasons?
practice.hint: With no decomposers, nothing goes back into the soil. Take away 3 twice.
practice.explain: {a} − 3 − 3 = {=a-6}. Without decomposers the used nutrients stay locked in dead leaves and never return.

practice.prompt: Why will a plastic bag not rot in a compost bin?
choices: It was never alive, so decomposers cannot feed on it
practice.hint: What kind of things can decomposers feed on?
practice.explain: Decomposers only feed on things that were once alive. Plastic is made from oil, so it lasts for hundreds of years.

pool.prompt: Which shows matter moving round a cycle?
choices: Air and soil → grass → rabbit → decomposers → air and soil
pool.hint: A cycle comes back to where it started.
pool.explain: Matter starts in the air and soil, goes into a plant, then an animal, then decomposers, and back. The sun gives energy, not matter.

pool.prompt: Where does grass get most of the matter it grows from?
choices: Carbon dioxide from the air and water
pool.hint: Think about the gas plants take in through their leaves.
pool.explain: Most of a plant's mass is built from carbon dioxide and water. The soil gives a small amount of minerals. Sunlight is energy, not matter.

pool.prompt: What would happen in a wood with no decomposers?
choices: Dead leaves would pile up and plants would run short of nutrients
pool.hint: Who returns nutrients to the soil?
pool.explain: Without decomposers, nothing breaks down dead matter. Nutrients stay locked in dead leaves, so the soil runs out.

pool.prompt: {=a*100} g of fallen apples rot in a box. After a month {=b*10} g of apple is left. How many grams went into the soil and air?
pool.hint: The matter that left the apples went somewhere. Find the difference.
pool.explain: {=a*100} − {=b*10} = {=a*100-b*10} g went into the soil and air. The total is still {=a*100} g.

pool.prompt: How does matter from a rabbit get back into the air?
choices: It breathes out carbon dioxide, and decomposers break down its body
It cannot: animals keep matter forever
Only by being eaten by a fox
pool.hint: Animals breathe out a gas. Decomposers also give gas to the air.
pool.explain: Rabbits breathe out carbon dioxide every day. When they die, decomposers break down the body and give carbon dioxide back too.

pool.prompt: Mia says rotting destroys the leaves. What is wrong?
choices: The matter moves into the soil and air; it is not destroyed
pool.hint: Weigh what is left plus what went to the soil and air.
pool.explain: Rotting changes the leaves into carbon dioxide, water and soil nutrients. The total amount of matter stays the same.

pool.prompt: Which job do worms do in the cycle?
choices: They feed on dead leaves and help break them down
pool.hint: Where do worms live and what do they eat?
pool.explain: Worms pull dead leaves into the soil and eat them, helping fungi and bacteria break them down into nutrients.

pool.prompt: A compost heap starts with {a} kg of garden waste. A year later decomposers have turned it into {b} kg of compost. In a simple model, how many kg went into the air?
pool.hint: Matter is not lost. What is not in the compost went into the air as carbon dioxide and water.
pool.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} kg went into the air as carbon dioxide and water. Compost plus air is still {a} kg.

pool.prompt: Which will NOT rot in a compost heap?
pool.hint: Was it ever part of a living thing?
pool.explain: Glass was never alive, so decomposers cannot feed on it. Cardboard is made from trees, so it rots.
